tonkatsu.name: Tonkatsu
tonkatsu.summary: A Japanese deep-fried, breaded pork cutlet that became popular as part of Western-style cuisine introduced to Japan.

yakiniku.name: Yakiniku
yakiniku.summary: A Japanese term for grilled bite-sized meat and vegetables cooked over a flame, a style whose modern form derives from Korean barbecue.

jiaozi.name: Gyōza
jiaozi.summary: The Japanese name for a variety of Chinese jiaozi dumplings, introduced to Japan after World War II by returning Japanese colonizers from China.

calpis.name: Calpis
calpis.summary: A Japanese probiotic milk beverage, lightly acidic and yogurt-like, made by lactic acid fermentation and sold as a concentrate to dilute with water.

okara-food.name: Okara
okara-food.summary: The pulp of insoluble soybean parts left over from making soy milk and tofu, used in traditional cuisines of Japan, Korea and China.

sunjae.name: Sunjae
sunjae.summary: A Jogye Order Buddhist nun born in 1956, known as Korea's first master of temple cuisine and an international promoter of Korean food.

sinheungsa.name: Sinheungsa
sinheungsa.summary: A head temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, located on Seoraksan mountain within Seoraksan National Park in South Korea.

yayoi-kusama.name: Yayoi Kusama
yayoi-kusama.summary: A Japanese artist (1929-2026) known for sculpture, installation and polka-dot motifs, ranked among the world's top-selling female artists and a major influence on pop art.

yoshitomo-nara.name: Yoshitomo Nara
yoshitomo-nara.summary: A Japanese artist born in 1959, known worldwide for paintings of 'big-headed girls' whose childlike cuteness carries a dark humor.

hiroshi-sugimoto.name: Hiroshi Sugimoto
hiroshi-sugimoto.summary: A Japanese photographer and architect, born 1948, who leads the Tokyo-based architectural firm New Material Research Laboratory.

chiharu-shiota.name: Chiharu Shiota
chiharu-shiota.summary: Japanese performance and installation artist, born 1972 and based in Berlin since 1996, who represented Japan at the 2015 Venice Biennale.

daid-moriyama.name: Daidō Moriyama
daid-moriyama.summary: A Japanese photographer, born 1938, known for raw black-and-white street photography of postwar urban Japan and his association with the avant-garde photography magazine Provoke.

kenz-tange.name: Kenzō Tange
kenz-tange.summary: Japanese architect (1913–2005) renowned for blending traditional Japanese style with modernism, notably the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, and a mentor of the metabolist movement.

hiroshima-peace-memorial-museum.name: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum
hiroshima-peace-memorial-museum.summary: A museum in Hiroshima established in 1955 to document the atomic bombing of the city in World War II, designed by architect Kenzō Tange and visited by 53 million people between 1955 and 2005.

nihonga.name: Nihonga
nihonga.summary: A traditional Japanese painting style using mineral pigments on silk or paper, named in the Meiji period to distinguish it from Western-style oil painting.

heian-period.name: Heian period
heian-period.summary: The last division of classical Japanese history (794–1185), a peak of imperial court art and literature even though real power lay with the Fujiwara clan.

international-style.name: International Style
international-style.summary: A major architectural movement beginning in 1920s western Europe, marked by minimalism, functional design, and heavy use of glass, steel and concrete, dominant until the 1970s.

japan-art-academy.name: Japan Art Academy
japan-art-academy.summary: Japan's highest-ranking official arts organization, known as the Imperial Fine Arts Academy from 1919 and the Imperial Art Academy from 1937 before taking its current name after World War II.

mori-gai.name: Mori Ōgai
mori-gai.summary: Japanese army surgeon general, translator, novelist and poet (1862–1922) who introduced German literature to Japan and helped modernize Japanese literature.

japan-fine-arts-exhibition.name: Japan Fine Arts Exhibition
japan-fine-arts-exhibition.summary: Japanese art exhibition established in 1907, known over time as the Bunten, Teiten and Shinbunten before becoming today's Nitten, covering painting, sculpture, craft and calligraphy.

maebashi.name: Maebashi
maebashi.summary: Capital city of Gunma Prefecture in Japan, nicknamed the "City of Water, Greenery and Poets" for its natural setting and the poets it produced.

kunio-maekawa.name: Kunio Maekawa
kunio-maekawa.summary: Japanese architect (1905–1986) and key figure of postwar modernism who blended Japanese tradition with European modernist design, known for the Tokyo Bunka Kaikan and National Museum of Modern Art.

japan-art-association.name: Japan Art Association
japan-art-association.summary: Traditionalist Japanese art organization tracing back to 1879, which promoted exhibitions, later founded the Ueno Royal Museum, and today organizes the Praemium Imperiale award.

korean-people-s-army.name: Korean People's Army
korean-people-s-army.summary: Combined military forces of North Korea, commanded through the Workers' Party of Korea, with about 29.9% of the population serving actively, in reserve, or in a paramilitary role as of 2021.

kim-il-sung.name: Kim Il Sung
kim-il-sung.summary: Founder and leader of North Korea from 1948 until his death in 1994, who authorized the 1950 invasion of South Korea that began the Korean War.

syngman-rhee.name: Syngman Rhee
syngman-rhee.summary: The first president of South Korea, serving from 1948 to 1960, and earlier a Korean independence activist and head of Korea's provisional government.

manchuria.name: Manchuria
manchuria.summary: A historical region of Northeast Asia covering present-day Northeast China and parts of the Russian Far East, the homeland of the Manchu people who founded the Qing dynasty.

mukden-incident.name: Mukden incident
mukden-incident.summary: A staged 1931 explosion used by Japanese military personnel as a pretext to invade Manchuria, leading to the puppet state of Manchukuo.

manchukuo.name: Manchukuo
manchukuo.summary: A Japanese puppet state set up in Manchuria in 1932, nominally ruled by former Chinese emperor Puyi but with all real decisions made by Japanese officials, lasting until 1945.

wake-island.name: Wake Island
wake-island.summary: A coral atoll in the Pacific and unincorporated US territory, seized by Japan in a World War II battle in December 1941 and held until September 1945.

british-malaya.name: British Malaya
british-malaya.summary: Term for British-controlled territories on the lower Malay Peninsula and Singapore from the late 18th to mid-20th century, a major producer of tin and rubber before Japanese occupation in World War II.

battles-of-khalkhin-gol.name: Battle of Khalkhin Gol
battles-of-khalkhin-gol.summary: A 1939 series of border battles between Soviet-Mongolian and Japanese forces, decisively won by the Soviets under Georgy Zhukov, that discouraged Japan from further conflict with the USSR.

kwantung-army.name: Kwantung Army
kwantung-army.summary: A group army of the Imperial Japanese Army, formed in 1906 to secure Japan's Manchurian holdings; it engineered the puppet state of Manchukuo and fought in China before surrendering to Soviet forces in August 1945.

yalta-conference.name: Yalta Conference
yalta-conference.summary: A February 1945 meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin near Yalta in Crimea to plan the postwar reorganization of Germany and Europe.

mongolian-people-s-republic.name: Mongolian People's Republic
mongolian-people-s-republic.summary: Mongolia's communist state from 1924 to 1992, the world's second communist country and the Soviet Union's first and longest-lasting satellite state.

battle-of-leyte-gulf.name: Battle of Leyte Gulf
battle-of-leyte-gulf.summary: The largest naval battle of World War II, fought in 1944, in which the US Navy defeated Japan's remaining fleet during the Allied invasion of the Philippines; the first battle with organized kamikaze attacks.

okinawa-island.name: Okinawa Island
okinawa-island.summary: The largest of Japan's Ryukyu Islands, about 640 km south of Kyushu, strategically important to the US military since the Battle of Okinawa in World War II.

joseph-stalin.name: Joseph Stalin
joseph-stalin.summary: Soviet politician who ruled the Soviet Union from 1922 until his death in 1953, becoming its de facto dictator by the 1930s and formalizing Marxism–Leninism.

franklin-d-roosevelt.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
franklin-d-roosevelt.summary: 32nd U.S. president (1933–1945) and the longest-serving in American history, who led the country through the Great Depression and World War II.

truth-and-reconciliation-commission-sout.name: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Korea)
truth-and-reconciliation-commission-sout.summary: A South Korean governmental body established in 2005 to investigate atrocities from Japan's rule of Korea in 1910 through the end of authoritarian rule in 1993.

bodo-league-massacre.name: Bodo League massacre
bodo-league-massacre.summary: Mass killing of alleged communists and sympathizers by South Korean forces in summer 1950 during the Korean War, with death toll estimates between 60,000 and 200,000.

stavka.name: Stavka
stavka.summary: The name for the high command of the armed forces in Imperial Russia, the Soviet Union, and present-day Ukraine.

roks-cheonan.name: ROKS Cheonan
roks-cheonan.summary: Name shared by two South Korean Navy warships: a Pohang-class corvette in service from 1989 to 2010, and a Daegu-class frigate commissioned in 2023.

yeonpyeongdo.name: Yeonpyeongdo
yeonpyeongdo.summary: A group of South Korean islands in the Yellow Sea, about 80 km west of Incheon, known for its crab fishery.

hanja.name: Hanja
hanja.summary: Chinese characters adapted to write Korean, used for most Korean writing until Hangul's promulgation in 1446 and still seen occasionally today.

ezra-pound.name: Ezra Pound
ezra-pound.summary: American poet and critic (1885-1972), a leading figure of early modernist poetry who shaped the work of Eliot, Joyce and Hemingway, and later collaborated with Fascist Italy in World War II.

t-s-eliot.name: T. S. Eliot
t-s-eliot.summary: A modernist poet, essayist and playwright (1888–1965) awarded the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature, known for works including The Waste Land and for reshaping English-language poetry.

meiji-era.name: Meiji era
meiji-era.summary: Period of Japanese history (1868–1912) under Emperor Meiji, when Japan moved from an isolated feudal society to a modern, industrialized world power.

yasunari-kawabata.name: Yasunari Kawabata
yasunari-kawabata.summary: A Japanese novelist (1899-1972) whose lyrical prose won him the 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first Japanese author to receive it.

kenzabur-e.name: Kenzaburō Ōe
kenzabur-e.summary: Japanese writer (1935–2023) whose work addressed nuclear weapons, social non-conformism and existentialism; he won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Literature.

jeong-ji-yong.name: Jeong Ji-yong
jeong-ji-yong.summary: A Korean poet and translator of English poetry (1902 – c. 1950), praised for opening new poetic possibilities through precise imagery and tempered sentiment.

doshisha-university.name: Doshisha University
doshisha-university.summary: A private university in Kyoto, Japan, founded in 1875 and one of the country's oldest private institutions of higher learning.

natsume-s-seki.name: Natsume Sōseki
natsume-s-seki.summary: Japanese novelist, poet and scholar (1867 to 1916), often called the first modern novelist of Japan, known for works including I Am a Cat, Botchan and Kokoro.

naoya-shiga.name: Naoya Shiga
naoya-shiga.summary: A Japanese writer (1883–1971) active in the Taishō and Shōwa periods, known for a lucid, straightforward style and strongly autobiographical fiction.

k-b-abe.name: Kōbō Abe
k-b-abe.summary: A 20th-century Japanese novelist, playwright and director best known for the 1962 novel The Woman in the Dunes, later made into an award-winning film; he died in 1993 aged 68.

haruki-murakami.name: Haruki Murakami
haruki-murakami.summary: Japanese writer born 1949 whose novels, including Norwegian Wood and The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, have sold millions of copies worldwide and won numerous international literary prizes.

o-seyeong.name: O Seyeong
o-seyeong.summary: A South Korean poet, critic and professor at Seoul National University, born in 1942, winner of several major Korean poetry prizes including the Manhae Literature Prize.

donald-keene.name: Donald Keene
donald-keene.summary: American-born scholar (1922–2019) who became a leading historian and translator of Japanese literature, taught at Columbia for over fifty years, and took Japanese citizenship late in life.

the-pleasures-of-japanese-literature.name: The Pleasures of Japanese Literature
the-pleasures-of-japanese-literature.summary: 1988 nonfiction book by Donald Keene introducing key themes in Japanese literature and aesthetics, such as wabi and mono no aware, for students and general readers.

kenjiro-takayanagi.name: Kenjiro Takayanagi
kenjiro-takayanagi.summary: Japanese engineer (1899–1990) who built the world's first all-electronic television receiver and is called the father of Japanese television.

yi-so-yeon.name: Yi So-yeon
yi-so-yeon.summary: A South Korean astronaut and biotechnologist, born 1978, who in 2008 became the first South Korean to fly into space, spending about eleven days there.

soyuz-tma-12.name: Soyuz TMA-12
soyuz-tma-12.summary: A Russian Soyuz mission that launched to the International Space Station on 8 April 2008 and landed on 24 October 2008.

isdb.name: ISDB
isdb.summary: Japanese digital broadcasting standard for television and radio that replaced older analog systems, launched in Japan in 2003 and later adopted in South America and the Philippines.

ntsc-j.name: NTSC-J
ntsc-j.summary: The analogue television standard used in Japan from 1960, based on the US NTSC system, replaced by digital broadcasting between 2011 and 2012.

jaxa.name: JAXA
jaxa.summary: Japan's national space and aeronautics agency, formed in 2003 by merging three earlier organisations; runs missions like Hayabusa and operates the H3 launch vehicle.

kib-iss-module.name: Kibō
kib-iss-module.summary: Japan's science module for the International Space Station, the largest single ISS pressurized module by volume, launched in pieces on Space Shuttle missions in 2008 and 2009.

h-ii-transfer-vehicle.name: H-II Transfer Vehicle (HTV)
h-ii-transfer-vehicle.summary: An expendable Japanese cargo spacecraft, also called Kounotori, used from 2009 to 2020 to resupply the International Space Station, especially its Japanese Kibō laboratory module.

kompsat-1.name: Arirang-1
kompsat-1.summary: South Korean satellite (KOMPSAT-1) launched in 1999, the first satellite built primarily by South Korean engineers, named after the folk song Arirang.

kompsat-2.name: Arirang-2
kompsat-2.summary: South Korean Earth observation satellite (KOMPSAT-2) launched in 2006, named after the folk song Arirang, able to identify individual vehicles on the ground.

akihiko-hoshide.name: Akihiko Hoshide
akihiko-hoshide.summary: A Japanese engineer and JAXA astronaut who became the third Japanese person to walk in space in 2012 and later served as a commander of the International Space Station.

j-stage.name: J-STAGE
j-stage.summary: An electronic platform run by the Japan Science and Technology Agency for publishing and disseminating Japanese academic journals, proceedings and reports.

douglas-macarthur.name: Douglas MacArthur
douglas-macarthur.summary: American general (1880–1964) who commanded Allied forces in the Pacific during World War II, oversaw the occupation of Japan, and led UN forces in the Korean War.

gojong-of-korea.name: Gojong
gojong-of-korea.summary: Penultimate Korean monarch (1852–1919), ruling 1864–1907 first as king of Joseon and then as the first emperor of the Korean Empire, amid growing Japanese pressure.

korea-under-japanese-rule.name: Chōsen
korea-under-japanese-rule.summary: Name used for Korea as a colony of the Empire of Japan from 1910 to 1945, being the Japanese reading of 'Joseon'.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

japan-korea-treaty-of-1905.name: Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905
japan-korea-treaty-of-1905.summary: A 1905 treaty, also called the Eulsa Treaty, that stripped Korea of its diplomatic sovereignty and made it a Japanese protectorate, following Japan's victory in the Russo-Japanese War.

japan-self-defense-forces.name: Japan Self-Defense Forces
japan-self-defense-forces.summary: Japan's military forces, comprising ground, maritime and air branches, created in 1954 after the postwar constitution renouncing war was reinterpreted amid Cold War tensions.

treaty-of-san-francisco.name: Treaty of San Francisco
treaty-of-san-francisco.summary: 1951 treaty formally ending the state of war between Japan and 49 Allied nations after World War II, restoring Japan's sovereignty.

greater-east-asia-co-prosperity-sphere.name: Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere
greater-east-asia-co-prosperity-sphere.summary: A pan-Asian union Japan tried to build during World War II, covering Japan, Korea, Manchukuo, China and later parts of Southeast Asia, presented as economic cooperation but used as propaganda for Japanese dominance.

nanp-islands.name: Nanpō Islands
nanp-islands.summary: A chain of Pacific islands south of Japan's main archipelago, administered by Tokyo, once claimed by Japan, Spain and Britain before returning fully to Japanese control in 1968.

ryukyu-islands.name: Ryukyu Islands
ryukyu-islands.summary: A chain of Japanese islands stretching from Kyushu to Taiwan, divided between Kagoshima and Okinawa prefectures, with Okinawa Island as the largest.

karafuto-prefecture.name: Karafuto Prefecture
karafuto-prefecture.summary: A Japanese colonial prefecture established in 1907 to govern southern Sakhalin after the Russo-Japanese War, occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1945.

sakhalin.name: Sakhalin
sakhalin.summary: Large island in Northeast Asia, now part of Russia, whose ownership was contested among China, Russia, and Japan over the past millennium.

mainland-japan.name: Naichi
mainland-japan.summary: Pre-war official term for Japan's core territory, distinguishing it from overseas possessions such as Taiwan, Korea and Karafuto.

marvin-tokayer.name: Marvin Tokayer
marvin-tokayer.summary: American rabbi and author who served as a US Air Force chaplain in Japan, then on the Lubavitcher Rebbe's advice spent eight years there as Japan's only rabbi; he now serves as a rabbi in Great Neck, New York.

tripartite-pact.name: Tripartite Pact
tripartite-pact.summary: A defensive alliance signed by Germany, Italy and Japan in Berlin on 27 September 1940, later joined by several other countries, formally uniting the Axis powers.

kyoto-school.name: Kyoto School
kyoto-school.summary: A Japanese philosophical movement centered at Kyoto University that blended Western philosophy with East Asian religious and moral thought, beginning around 1913 with founder Kitarō Nishida.

taish-era.name: Taishō era
taish-era.summary: A period of Japanese history from 1912 to 1926, marked by a shift toward democratic government known as Taishō Democracy.

kitar-nishida.name: Kitarō Nishida
kitar-nishida.summary: A Japanese moral philosopher who lived from 1870 to 1945 and founded the Kyoto School of philosophy, teaching at Kyoto University after graduating from the University of Tokyo in 1894.

tetsur-watsuji.name: Tetsuro Watsuji
tetsur-watsuji.summary: Japanese historian and moral philosopher who lived from 1889 to 1960.

german-idealism.name: German idealism
german-idealism.summary: A philosophical movement in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, developed from Kant's work and including Fichte, Schelling and Hegel.

neo-confucianism.name: Neo-Confucianism
neo-confucianism.summary: A revival of Confucianism as an ethical, social and religious system that dominated Chinese philosophy from the 13th to 19th century, developed under Zhu Xi during the Song dynasty.

analytic-philosophy.name: Analytic philosophy
analytic-philosophy.summary: A broad school of Western philosophy emphasizing rigorous argument, logic and language, contrasted with continental philosophy and dominant since the early 20th century in figures like Frege, Russell and Wittgenstein.

post-structuralism.name: Post-structuralism
post-structuralism.summary: A philosophical movement that questions the objectivity and stability of the structures proposed by structuralism, viewing them as shaped by broader systems of power.

t-k-seung.name: T. K. Seung
t-k-seung.summary: A Korean-American philosopher and literary critic (1930–2022) whose work spanned ethics, political philosophy and literary criticism; he was a professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

cheongju.name: Cheongju
cheongju.summary: The capital and largest city of North Chungcheong Province in South Korea.

new-criticism.name: New Criticism
new-criticism.summary: A mid-20th-century American literary theory movement emphasizing close reading of texts as self-contained works, led by figures like John Crowe Ransom and Cleanth Brooks.

s-nggyun-gwan.name: Sŏnggyun'gwan
s-nggyun-gwan.summary: The foremost educational institution in Korea during the late Goryeo and Joseon dynasties, where a rite honoring Confucius is still performed twice a year at its Seoul campus.

governor-general-of-ch-sen.name: Governor-General of Chōsen
governor-general-of-ch-sen.summary: The chief administrator of Japan's colonial government in Korea from 1910 to 1945, appointed from Tokyo and responsible for infrastructure, justice, censorship and suppressing Korean independence efforts.

nintendo-entertainment-system.name: Family Computer
nintendo-entertainment-system.summary: Nintendo's first programmable home video game console, released in Japan in 1983 and later sold internationally from 1985 as the Nintendo Entertainment System.

korean-new-year.name: Seollal
korean-new-year.summary: Traditional Korean festival marking the first day of the lunar new year, one of the most important holidays for Koreans, marked with family visits, ancestral rites and traditional food and dress.

samguk-yusa.name: Samguk yusa
samguk-yusa.summary: A collection of Korean legends and historical accounts compiled by the Buddhist monk Il-yeon around 1280; it holds the earliest surviving record of the Dangun founding legend.

kim-dae-jung.name: Kim Dae-jung
kim-dae-jung.summary: South Korean president from 1998 to 2003 (1924–2009), a former dissident who was imprisoned, exiled and nearly killed for opposing military dictatorship.

mu-shaman.name: Mudang
mu-shaman.summary: The Korean term for a shaman in Korean shamanism, used mostly for female practitioners who lead welfare rituals called gut.

onisaburo-deguchi.name: Onisaburo Deguchi
onisaburo-deguchi.summary: Japanese religious leader (1871–1948) who, alongside his mother-in-law Nao Deguchi, co-founded the Oomoto movement, serving as its 'Holy Teacher.'

oomoto.name: Oomoto
oomoto.summary: Shinto-based Japanese new religion founded in the 1890s by Deguchi Nao and Deguchi Onisaburō, notable for promoting Esperanto and interfaith dialogue.

tsunesabur-makiguchi.name: Tsunesaburō Makiguchi
tsunesabur-makiguchi.summary: Japanese educator (1871–1944) who founded the Value-Creating Education Society, the predecessor of today's Soka Gakkai.

soka-gakkai.name: Soka Gakkai
soka-gakkai.summary: A Japanese Buddhist movement founded in 1930 on the teachings of the 13th-century priest Nichiren, later influential in Japanese politics through its affiliated party Komeito.

state-shinto.name: State Shinto
state-shinto.summary: Imperial Japan's use of Shinto as state ideology, emphasizing the emperor's divine status and treating shrines as patriotic rather than religious institutions.

pink-lady-duo.name: Pink Lady
pink-lady-duo.summary: A Japanese female pop duo of the late 1970s and early 1980s, one of only two Japanese acts to reach the Billboard Top 40 and the first to perform in Seoul.

imase.name: Imase
imase.summary: A Japanese singer-songwriter, born in 2000, who debuted in 2021 and became known worldwide for his viral 2022 single 'Night Dancer.'

komeito.name: Komeito
komeito.summary: A centrist Japanese political party linked to the Soka Gakkai religious movement, founded in 1964, that long served as junior coalition partner to the Liberal Democratic Party.

japanese-new-religions.name: Shinshūkyō
japanese-new-religions.summary: Japanese term for new religious movements founded since the mid-19th century, mostly shaped by older Buddhist and Shinto traditions along with some foreign influences.

seiko-matsuda.name: Seiko Matsuda
seiko-matsuda.summary: A Japanese singer-songwriter born in 1962, one of the most popular idols of the 1980s, dubbed the 'Eternal Idol' for her long career and record sales.

aoi-sangoshou.name: Aoi Sangoshou
aoi-sangoshou.summary: The second single by Japanese singer Seiko Matsuda, reaching number 2 on Japan's Oricon chart and selling over 600,000 copies.

newjeans.name: NewJeans
newjeans.summary: A South Korean girl group formed by ADOR in 2022, known for hits like "Attention," "Hype Boy" and "Ditto," with a style recalling 1990s and 2000s pop.

maeil-broadcasting-network.name: MBN
maeil-broadcasting-network.summary: South Korean cable TV network founded in 1993, operated by the Maeil Business Newspaper.
